alalal-c50541-d1e104.summary: Rubric of Article 25: whether two spirits can be in one spiritual place without crowding each other.

alalal-c50541-d1e115.summary: Introduces the question on Lombard's (Augustine's) statement that many spirits here would not crowd the place.

alalal-c50541-d1e129.summary: Objection from Damascene, who defines an intelligible place where an incorporeal nature is and acts, not bodily contained: as bodily place is to body, so intelligible place is to spirit; bodies cannot share a place without crowding, so neither can spirits share an intelligible place.
concepts: analogy of bodily and spiritual place

alalal-c50541-d1e167.summary: Asks what Damascene means by intelligible place: not an intelligible nature like God or an angel, since one angel does not enclose another and Lombard denies that God is properly a place; nor the place in which an intellectual nature is, for then it would not differ from bodily place.

alalal-c50541-d1e202.summary: Solution: place is said properly or by metaphor from its properties. Metaphorically a spiritual nature can be a place, as the soul is the place of species (De anima III), since it preserves them incorruptibly and they rest in it; likewise God is the intelligible place of angels, who run within God wherever sent (Bede), since he encompasses them by power. Properly, place is definitive or circumscriptive; Damascene's intellectual place is definitive place, named from its relation to an intellectual nature, as bodily place is named from the body it contains per se or per accidens.
claims: God is the metaphorical intelligible place of angels, as the soul is the place of species.
Damascene's intellectual place is definitive place, named from its relation to an angel.

alalal-c50541-d1e287.summary: Reply to the first objection: Lombard means place with bodily containment; spirits do not fill it, so they can be together with any body and do not crowd each other. But intelligible place, defined by its relation to an intellectual nature determined to it by its operation, cannot bear that relation to two angels, so two angels cannot be in the same place.
claims: Spirits do not crowd bodily place, but two angels cannot occupy the same definitive place.

alalal-c50541.summary: Article 25 asks how Lombard can say that many spirits would not crowd a place, given Damascene's notion of an intelligible place for spirits, analogous to bodily place. Albert distinguishes metaphorical and proper place. Metaphorically, a spiritual nature can be a place: the soul for species, and God for the angels, who run within him wherever they are sent. Properly, place is circumscriptive or definitive, and Damascene's intellectual place is definitive place, named from its relation to the angel defined in it by its operation. Spirits do not fill or crowd bodily place, as Lombard says, but two angels cannot share one definitive place, since that relation cannot hold of two.
claims: Spirits do not crowd bodily place, since they do not fill it.
Two angels cannot be in the same definitive place.
God is metaphorically the intelligible place of angels.
